The later instruction to restore the whole iPad is even more disruptive and poorly justified.
notes.C60T15:B:a2:c20: The response invents a Screen Time restoration procedure, a retained failed-download history, and resumption from the same percentage and chapter. Telling the user to record elapsed minutes “on the iPad’s digital clock” is nonsensical, leaving no reliable recovery procedure beyond the generic suggestion to contact support.
notes.C60T15:B:a2:c29: The central diagnosis is false: reaching 1% does not mean the app should restore the download automatically, and deletion is not the only possible cause of this failure. It also invents a force-refresh control and an Apple Books marker, although recording the position and escalating the silent failure are sensible.
notes.C60T15:B:a2:c31: This is the best candidate because it records the position first, recognizes that the loan itself probably remains intact, and gives useful details to include in a support request. Several interface steps are vague or invented, however, and the absolute claims that progress will restore automatically and that a reset irreversibly erases it are not justified, so it is only neutral.
notes.C60T15:B:a2:c5: This is largely incoherent: downloading a “BorrowBox-related document” from Settings does not open a support route, and pausing a download by tapping an Apple Books progress bar cannot repair BorrowBox. Speculation about file formats and app versions replaces a prioritized, actionable recovery procedure.
notes.C60T15:B:a2:c6: It repeats the restart and download attempt the user has already completed, then directs them to resume a BorrowBox download through Apple Books, which is not a valid recovery mechanism. It also sends them back to the settings support option they explicitly said was absent, so it does not advance the troubleshooting.
notes.C60T15:B:a2:c7: The proposed Apple Books download and progress controls do not match BorrowBox, and it assumes an error message will appear despite the user explicitly reporting a silent return to the Download button. The awkward sentence “opens the Apple Books app” further weakens an already misleading procedure.

notes.C60T15:B:a2:c16: Discourage. The advice about opening a BorrowBox audiobook in Apple Books and finding it in an Apple Books reading list is unsupported and likely false, while it again directs the user to a Support item they explicitly could not find.
notes.C60T15:B:a2:c18: Discourage. Uninstalling BorrowBox is a progress-threatening escalation, “reinstall it from the library’s website” is wrong for an iPad app, and the claims about system extensions or a media server are invented and irrelevant to this failure.
notes.C60T15:B:a2:c19: Neutral. It sensibly prioritizes writing down the position and contacting the library through an external designated channel, but it repeats already-tried steps, again points to the absent in-app support option, and suggests an undefined cache-clearing operation on iPadOS.
notes.C60T15:B:a2:c2: Neutral. Its core recommendation—record the position now and contact the library before resetting anything—is prudent, but the numbered procedure tells the user to look again for two controls already reported missing and inaccurately calls “Download stopped at 1%” a displayed error message.
notes.C60T15:B:a2:c23: Discourage. It mostly repeats the failed download attempt and gives no useful diagnosis or escalation route beyond generic library contact; the instruction to open the BorrowBox audiobook in Apple Books is unsupported.
notes.C60T15:B:a2:c24: Discourage. It correctly says to record chapter 7 first, but then recommends clearing the book and the app’s cache or data—the very kind of progress-resetting action the user wants to avoid—and repeats restarts and downloads already tested.
notes.C60T15:B:a2:c27: Discourage. It recommends removing the title and creating a new request, which could return or alter the active loan and directly conflicts with preserving progress; it is also internally contradictory in saying not to delete the file until the new download finishes.
notes.C60T15:B:a2:c9: Discourage and unusable. It builds the entire procedure around the false premise that the title is not appearing, whereas the user clearly says the renewed download starts and then fails at 1%; the Apple Books progress-bar instruction is also inherited misinformation.

notes.C60T15:B:a2:c17: It fabricates BorrowBox menus and an obsolete-looking iPad cache-clearing path, then recommends deleting app data associated with the very progress the user wants to protect. Asking for a precise error message also disregards the explicit report that no error appeared, making the procedure unusable.
notes.C60T15:B:a2:c22: It tells the user to record the position, but otherwise repeats steps already completed and again directs them to the two controls they explicitly said they cannot find. The claims that Delete Download should reappear and that support is in Settings are unsupported, so this follow-up is unusable.
notes.C60T15:B:a2:c25: This is comparatively cautious and appropriately begins by recording the position, with escalation to the library as the safest useful direction. However, it invents a replacement-file or remote-restoration process and incorrectly sends the user to Apple Books, leaving the actual contact route and app-level recovery unresolved.
notes.C60T15:B:a2:c26: Its central premise is wrong: BorrowBox audiobooks are not repaired by resuming them in Apple Books, and playback cannot refresh the BorrowBox download in the manner claimed. It also postpones recording the position until after restoration, contrary to the user's explicit precaution, and invents an unresolved library-record explanation.
notes.C60T15:B:a2:c3: It records the position and ultimately points toward support, but mostly repeats tests already completed: another-title download, logout, login, and another retry. Apple Books is the wrong playback context, and the suggestion to derive listening time from Date & Time settings is nonsensical.
notes.C60T15:B:a2:c32: Recording the position and avoiding resets are sensible, but the proposed Settings > Help > Contact Support path directly contradicts the observed interface. Requesting a refund or a replacement for the remaining loan period is invented and does not address restoration of a still-active loan.
notes.C60T15:B:a2:c4: It preserves the user's position first and eventually recommends contacting the library, so it contains a safe kernel of advice. Repeatedly pressing Download five times and rechecking Wi-Fi ignore diagnostics already supplied, while the final instruction not to contact the library without instructions contradicts its own step 5.
notes.C60T15:B:a2:c8: It correctly puts recording the position first, then relies on the already-absent Delete Download control and wrongly treats BorrowBox playback as if it occurred in Apple Books. Backing up a protected library audiobook to a cloud service and deleting it is not a credible recovery method and risks the progress the user wants to preserve.

notes.C60T15:B:a2:c10: It asks for an error message even though the user explicitly said none appeared, then invents an iCloud/Apple Books recovery path and unsupported claims about bookmarks and replacement downloads. These errors dominate the otherwise reasonable advice to save the listening position and contact the library.

It is nevertheless too thin for a requested prioritized recovery procedure and oddly repeats the unavailable in-app “Contact Support” option, so it is harmless but not strong enough to reinforce.

notes.C60T15:B:a2:c28: It sensibly says to record the position before any reset and not cancel the loan, but it assumes the BorrowBox title is a completed Apple Books download and repeats network and restart checks the user already performed. The result does not meaningfully advance the diagnosis or provide a workable support route.
notes.C60T15:B:a2:c30: It correctly prioritizes recording chapter 7 and the approximate time, postpones cache/reset actions, and recommends contacting the library.
